topics.title: 2014 amc 10a #25 solution question
topics.text:
Heres the problem:

The number $5^{867}$ is between $2^{2013}$ and $2^{2014}$. How many pairs of integers $(m,n)$ are there such that $1\leq m\leq 2012$ and \[5^n<2^m<2^{m+2}<5^{n+1}?\]$\textbf{(A) }278\qquad \textbf{(B) }279\qquad \textbf{(C) }280\qquad \textbf{(D) }281\qquad \textbf{(E) }282\qquad$

Here's the solution:

Between any two consecutive powers of $5$ there are either $2$ or $3$ powers of $2$ (because $2^2<5^1<2^3$). Consider the intervals $(5^0,5^1),(5^1,5^2),\dots (5^{866},5^{867})$. We want the number of intervals with $3$ powers of $2$.



From the given that $2^{2013}<5^{867}<2^{2014}$, we know that these $867$ intervals together have $2013$ powers of $2$. Let $x$ of them have $2$ powers of $2$ and $y$ of them have $3$ powers of $2$. Thus we have the system \[x+y=867\]\[2x+3y=2013\]from which we get $y=279$, so the answer is $\boxed{\textbf{(B)}}$.



I don't understand how they got this part:

Click to reveal hidden textBetween any two consecutive powers of $5$ there are either $2$ or $3$ powers of $2$ (because $2^2<5^1<2^3$)


Could someone explain it?

topics.title: AM-GM question
topics.text:
This is an AM-GM question I was looking at and one part of its solution is curious to me.



[quote]Minimise $x^2+y^2+z^2$ subject to $x,y,z$ > 0 and $xyz$ = 1.



By AM-GM,

$x^2+y^2+z^2$ ≥ 3$\sqrt[3]{(x^2)(y^2)(z^2)}$

=$\sqrt[3]{(xyz)^2}$

=1.



The minimum occurs when $x^2 = y^2 = z^2$, i.e., when $x=y=z$ = 1.[/quote]



My one question is why it's okay to remove the 3 that's multiplying the cubic root. I understand that if the LHS is ≥ 3 times a number, then the LHS is certainly ≥ that number by itself, but it still seems an important part of the inequality, i.e. that it multiples by 1 when the cubic root resolves to leave the RHS as 3, and not 1. Perhaps this is a simple oversight, perhaps I fundamentally misunderstand AM-GM, but I was hoping someone could point me in the right direction.

topics.title: I have kind of a weird question
topics.text:
Heres the problem:

K is the set of natural numbers with the property that every element of K is not divisible by 3 or 4. But if a number is divisible by 3 or 4 and is also divisible by 5, the number is in K (like 15, 20, 60,...). Find the 79th smallest member of K.

My solution:

So you notice the sequence "repeats" when a multiple of 60 pops up. the first time 60 pops up you can use PIE to find there are 36 terms in the sequence. so the 72nd term will be 120. Now you can count to the 79 term. However, you could also find the 7th term and add it to 120. The 7th term is 13 so the answer is 133



My question is why in my solution, you can say that the sequence repeats after a multiple of 60.

If you don't understand what I'm trying to ask, think about the question: How many multiples of 3 and 4 are under 61(sol includes 60, but not 61). You can solve by saying there are 6 multiples of 3 and 4 every 12 so there are 30 multiples of 3 and 4 under 60.

But why can you do this? Why does it repeat after 12?

I think it has something to do with CRT

topics.title: Can 3D shapes always intersect every one of each other?
topics.text:
Imagine you have a fixed number of 3D shapes that can be as wacky as your imagination can take you, but not one bit of the shape can be infinitely flat, long, small, or broken. In other words, you can only have 3D shapes that don't have a 2 dimensional object sticking out or line segment sticking out, and the shape cannot be infinite in 3D space nor be a single point. The shape also cannot be broken. But apart from that, you can have 3D shapes that can be crazier than anyone's imagination could ever be. They can be curved, straight, they could look like a highway system! They can look insane! I will call these shapes "perfect shapes" in this post.



What I was interested in was: If we have a fixed number of these perfect shapes and made them be shaped like anything, will we always be able to make every one of them touch every other one of them? I simply used my imagination. I imagined: Take millions and millions of spheres in 3D space. Billions. Trillions. More. Now imagine string-like things coming out of each sphere and touching every other sphere. The strings can be as small as possible, but they cannot be 1 dimensional. They can very easily touch every other sphere. From here, it was obvious to me. When you have a fixed number of perfect shapes, you can always shape them so that every single shape touches every other shape.



But when I tried this with 2D shapes, it didn't work so well. The strings kept blocking each other, while in 3D space the strings have freedom to go where they need to go without blocking each other. It only worked with a small number of shapes.



But is this theory with 3D and 2D shapes true?
